Don Cherry & Okay Temiz :: Music for Turkish Theater 1970 Posted on August 13, 2026 August 13, 2026 In 1969 Istanbul, James Baldwin brought Don Cherry and Turkish percussionist Okay Temiz together to score Fortune and Men’s Eyes , a controversial play about gay love in an Istanbul prison. In Gowan Ring :: The Glinting Spade Posted on August 13, 2026 August 13, 2026 Some records evoke another era, and then there are those that seem untouched by chronology. Jan & Dean :: Save for a Rainy Day Posted on August 12, 2026 August 11, 2026 Far removed from Jan & Dean’s halcyon early days as surf-rock “California sound” architects, Save for a Rainy Day was a valiant attempt at a concept album revolving around summer thunderstorms and precipitation. Conceived as a solo effort to keep the duo’s name alive in Jan Berry’s medical absence, Dean Torrence and a series of key session players from the Wrecking Crew worked patchwork rain sound effects around lilting harmonies admirably reminiscent of their old collaborator Brian Wilson. Somber and cathartic, it’s an oddly whimsical sunshine pop trip for both dry and wet weather. Transmissions :: Dust-to-Digital Posted on August 12, 2026 August 12, 2026 Since 1999, Atlanta label ⁠Dust-to-Digital⁠ has created lavish boxsets, books, and collections of gospel, folk, blues, field recordings, and other sounds sourced from deep global archives. Nick Hakim :: I Can See Posted on August 11, 2026 August 10, 2026 A patient, deeply atmospheric work developed over more than five years, Nick Hakim’s I Can See finds the in-demand producer and songwriter distilling his expansive palette into something quieter, more intimate, and quietly elegant. Wild Havana :: Wild Havana (1977) Posted on August 11, 2026 August 11, 2026 In 1977, a Dutch multi-instrumentalist named Johan Smit tried to synthesize his adventures in 1970s music. Drawing on kraut, prog, jazz-funk and the ethnic rock experiments of Embryo and Popul Vuh, Smit and some of his friends put together one of the more weirdly compelling artifacts of the private press era. Wild Havana is at once retro and futuristic, looking backwards toward traditional sounds while anticipating the mutant funk and electro of the 1980s. It doesn’t all come together, but not coming together is what makes it all work. Wau Wau Collectif :: Teranga Posted on August 10, 2026 August 9, 2026 Originating in 2018 when Swedish music archaeologist Karl Jonas Winqvist brought together a group of local musicians, producers, and poets in the Senegalese fishing village of Toubab Dialaw, the Wau Wau Collectif has since felt like something too precious and magical to be real. Renascent , the first The Durutti Column record in over fifteen years, keeps us bumping into the bones inside that perfume, pushing Vini Reilly’s hazy summer aesthetics somewhere even more unperturbed and unpretentious. At 73, after a series of strokes that had theoretically compromised his ability to play, Reilly has made a record where all structure is just texture stretched thin enough, or all texture only structure slowed down. Beverly Glenn-Copeland :: Light of the Heavens Posted on August 9, 2026 August 9, 2026 Recorded shortly after his 1986 cult classic, Keyboard Fantasies , “Light of the Heavens” is a nearly lost relic by Beverly Glenn-Copeland. Existing in the same mesmeric electronic sphere of that album, the track features rippling synths and heavenly chants, as Glenn-Copeland sings lovingly of our infinite cosmic connection. A dazzling video for the song, also unearthed, features trance-like interpretive dance, celestial stained glass, and a bespectacled Glenn-Copeland draped in era appropriate silky headband and robe, singing of “the weaving stars of deepest night,” a paean to the master plan behind our mysterious existence. Twisted Teens :: Florida Water Blues Posted on August 7, 2026 August 3, 2026 The punk rock, blues-garage band known as Twisted Teens is moving at warp speed through music history straight on through to the future. This latest, Florida Water Blues , follows Blame the Clown by a few months and the self-titled by less than a year, and, never fear, there’s another one on the way. These people aren’t sitting around waiting, for fame, for money, for recognition. No they’re grabbing up music by the handfuls, mining 1930s electric blues licks and punk jackhammer beats and doo-woppy waltz time swirl and dropping them into a blender. This album ranges a little further afield than the previous two, suggesting that there will be more to Twisted Teens if you wait a bit, though they are already a whole fucking lot. Pax Nicholas and the Nettey Family :: Na Teef Know De Road of Teef Posted on August 6, 2026 July 29, 2026 Long obscured by Afrobeat lore and rescued from obscurity by Daptone Records in 2009, Pax Nicholas and the Nettey Family’s Na Teef Know De Road of Teef rides deep-pocket funk, burnished brass, and rolling polyrhythms across four tracks in just over 30 minutes. This festival is, and always has been, a vast departure from the life we’ve been told we have to live. That’s why it remains as special as it is. The people hosting this gathering are cut from the same rebellious cloth, as they dare to take risks where it counts, doing things their way, but never losing sight of what they originally set out to accomplish years ago.
